summary:
The anti-discrimination provision in force since 1 January 2007 makes anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not among the listed grounds. On the sourced account this made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Before that provision took effect, homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out, and he and his family then received threatening telephone calls; police refused to take the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012. The most recent documented assault in this record is the 2006 attack; no later instance is documented.

In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn. The group was not attacked anywhere else.

Hostility from elected officials is documented over a decade. The first gay pride march in 2005 provoked substantial controversy. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister and her partner, citing his religion. In July 2015 he demanded that Pride be banned, an event held two days before the national holiday; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality, and the singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. Av Rana has repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre. The most recent dated item of official hostility in this record is from July 2015; no later instance is documented.

Petitioning has been the main channel of advocacy. In November 2006, in a population of about 47,000, activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordic countries; neither existed at that date. After the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen, eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 signatures by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A separate petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.
tangentialFactors:
On the sourced account the Faroe Islands was the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, and only from 1 January 2007; the 2006 petitioners framed their demand explicitly as alignment with the rest of the Nordic countries.

The 2006 petition gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, with a further 2,000 collected offline by eight women in Tórshavn. The opposing petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures. These are raw signature counts, not per-capita measures of support.

Official hostility drew organised public pushback: when a Centre Party leader demanded in July 2015 that Pride be banned, the singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. The most recent dated item of either hostility or pushback in this record is from July 2015.

The only criminal penalty touching LGBT people in this inventory sits in the 1 January 2007 provision, whose listed grounds run to sexual orientation and stop there. Nothing in the sources shows a trans-specific offence, protection or penalty.

The Centre Party remains formally opposed to homosexuality as of July 2015 reporting, and its leader has repeatedly sought to move the Tórshavn pride parade out of the centre and compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters.

The 1 January 2007 provision governs residents' public statements, carrying a fine or up to two years' imprisonment for publicly threatening, insulting or degrading a group on the listed grounds. No prosecution or sentence under it appears in this inventory.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether a registered-partnership or same-sex marriage statute has been enacted since the November 2006 demand is unresolved in these sources. The inventory records only that neither existed at that date and that a separate petition gathered 1,262 signatures against same-sex marriage.

No trans-specific legal provision appears in this inventory: legal gender recognition, gender-marker rules, facilities access, healthcare access and any gender-identity ground in Faroese law are not sourced here. The assessment rests on sexual-orientation evidence and on the grounds listed in the 1 January 2007 provision.

Enforcement of the 1 January 2007 provision is unresolved: no prosecution, sentence, or police outcome under it is documented in these sources.

No trans-specific killing, assault or survey figure for trans people appears in this inventory. The violence documented is homophobic and dated 2005 and 2006, with the 2012 death of Rasmus Rasmussen following the 2006 attack.
